content_units: Month-Long Theme Arc: Ambition and Moral Compromise

This 4-week plan pairs one compact novel with one film or limited series each week, balancing readable length, sub-10-hour screen time, and variety across eras and countries. The sequence moves from social ascent, to corporate self-invention, to political corruption, to intimate ethical collapse.
Four-Week Reading-and-Screen Schedule
Week   Novel   Pages   Screen Pairing   Runtime   Origin Mix   Why This Pair Works
1     The Great Gatsby   by F. Scott Fitzgerald   180     Parasite   (film, 2019)   2h 12m   US + South Korea   Both examine class ambition, performance, and the rot beneath aspirational lifestyles.

2     The Talented Mr. Ripley   by Patricia Highsmith   336     Nightcrawler   (film, 2014)   1h 57m   US/UK novel + US film   These are sharp portraits of self-fashioning, deception, and success without conscience.

3     Chronicle of a Death Foretold   by Gabriel García Márquez   128     The King’s Man   (limited series substitute:   State of Play   miniseries, 2003)   6h   Colombia + UK   Both explore how social systems, public reputation, and institutional complicity enable moral failure.

4     The Remains of the Day   by Kazuo Ishiguro   258     A Separation   (film, 2011)   2h 3m   UK/Japan author + Iran film   Both focus on quiet compromise: people who call their choices duty, even when ethics are slipping.
Weekly Session Cards
Week 1: Glitter, Hunger, and the Cost of Climbing
Read:    The Great Gatsby
Watch:    Parasite
Rationale:   Each work turns status anxiety into suspense. One uses elegance and nostalgia, the other dark satire and shock, but both ask what ambition becomes when class mobility feels rigged.
Discussion prompts
- When does aspiration become manipulation?
- Which characters believe wealth will solve a moral problem?
- How do houses, rooms, and parties function as symbols of power?
- Do these stories criticize ambition itself, or only the systems around it?
Week 2: Reinvention Without a Conscience
Read:    The Talented Mr. Ripley
Watch:    Nightcrawler
Rationale:   This is the most direct week on ambition as predation. Ripley and Lou Bloom are both students of desire: they watch what society rewards, then erase any boundary that gets in the way.
Discussion prompts
- Why are these protagonists so compelling despite their behavior?
- Is talent presented as genuine skill, or as the ability to mimic what others value?
- What role does capitalism or social prestige play in excusing moral compromise?
- At what point did you stop hoping the protagonist would change?
Week 3: Public Knowledge, Private Evasion
Read:    Chronicle of a Death Foretold
Watch:    State of Play  (BBC miniseries, 6 episodes)

Rationale:   This week broadens the theme from individual ambition to communal and institutional failure. Both works show people navigating scandal, reputation, and responsibility while everyone senses wrongdoing and still allows it to continue.
Discussion prompts
- How do groups become morally passive even when many people know the truth?
- What matters more in these stories: justice, loyalty, or image?
- How does structure affect suspense when the audience already senses the outcome?
- Which compromises feel personal, and which feel systemic?
Week 4: Duty as an Alibi
Read:    The Remains of the Day
Watch:    A Separation

Rationale:   The final week shifts from flashy ambition to inward ethical erosion. These works are quieter and more painful, showing how compromise often hides inside professionalism, loyalty, family obligation, and self-protective narration.
Discussion prompts
- How do the characters use duty or propriety to avoid harder truths?
- Is moral compromise here a deliberate choice or gradual habit?
- Which story is more forgiving toward its characters?
- What does ambition look like when it is emotional, domestic, or social rather than financial?
Hosting Notes for a Bookstore Series
Option 1: Weekly evening salon   90-minute format with 20-minute opening context, 40-minute discussion, 30-minute audience Q&A   Best for regular community turnout
Event format
Option 2: Split-session model   Book discussion midweek, screen discussion on weekend   Best for longer audience engagement
Plan sessions
Option 3: Theme-first display table   Stack all four books with shelf talkers on “aspiration,” “image,” “class,” and “duty”   Best for in-store discovery
Display ideas
Quick Actions
Print reading list
Create event page
Selection Notes
- Page counts are standard approximate editions and may vary slightly by publisher.
- The screen selections all stay under   10 total hours   each.
- Country/era variation is built in across 1920s America, mid-century psychological crime, Latin American modernism, and late-20th-century/21st-century global cinema.
